nameStory: This little succulent gets its name from its beautiful pink flowers and its origins in the high mountains of Mongolia and surrounding Asian ranges. The 'stonecrop' part of its name comes from the plant family's amazing ability to grow in rocky crevices and stone walls where most other plants would give up - they literally 'crop up' among the stones!
description: Pink Mongolian stonecrop is a low-growing succulent perennial that forms spreading mats just 6 inches tall. It has thick, fleshy blue-gray leaves that feel rubbery to the touch and store water like a cactus does. In late summer, it produces clusters of small pink flowers that attract butterflies and bees. Unlike many succulents, this hardy plant loses its leaves in winter and regrows them each spring.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, succulent leaves that feel like soft rubber erasers and have a distinctive blue-gray or silvery-green color that stands out against other plants

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink star-shaped flowers clustered together in flat-topped bunches that appear in late summer, each flower having 5 pointed petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely getting taller than 6 inches but spreading outward like a living carpet

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Trailing stems that feel firm and slightly squishy, often rooting where they touch the ground to form new plants

habitat: In New England, pink Mongolian stonecrop is extremely rare, with only 2 recorded observations. When found, it's typically in rock gardens, stone walls, or well-drained rocky areas where it has been planted as an ornamental groundcover. It prefers sunny spots with excellent drainage and can tolerate poor, thin soils that would stress most other plants.

seasonality.spring: New blue-gray leaves emerge from the ground as thick, succulent rosettes that feel cool and rubbery to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full size and the plant spreads outward. Pink flower buds begin forming in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Pink flowers bloom in late summer to early fall, creating a carpet of tiny star-shaped blossoms that buzz with pollinating insects.
seasonality.winter: The plant goes completely dormant, with all above-ground parts dying back, leaving only underground roots to survive the cold.

funFact: This tough little plant can survive temperatures down to -40°F (USDA zone 2), making it one of the most cold-hardy succulents in the world - it's actually more freeze-tolerant than many trees!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other stonecrop species, but pink Mongolian stonecrop's distinctive blue-gray leaf color and trailing growth habit set it apart from the more upright, green-leaved stonecrops. Remember: blue-gray leaves that trail = Mongolian.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Mongolian' stonecrop, this plant actually grows wild across many Asian mountain ranges, not just Mongolia. The genus name Hylotelephium means 'live-forever,' referring to the plant's ability to survive in harsh conditions and its long-lived nature.
compareHints: Pink Mongolian stonecrop differs from its New England relatives like orpine and garden stonecrop by its trailing, mat-forming habit and distinctive blue-gray leaves. While orpine grows tall and upright with green leaves, and garden stonecrop forms clumps, pink Mongolian stonecrop spreads horizontally like a living carpet. Its cold tolerance also far exceeds that of most other stonecrops.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orpine differs from other stonecrops in its much larger size and robust growth habit - while most stonecrops are low, creeping plants, orpine stands tall and upright.
Garden stonecrop differs from its close relative orpine by having more distinctly spoon-shaped leaves and typically paler flowers.
Butterfly stonecrop is larger and showier than its relatives, reaching 2 feet tall versus the 6-12 inches of most other stonecrops in New England.
Compared to the common Orpine found throughout New England, Tatarinow's stonecrop is much smaller and more compact, staying under a foot tall versus Orpine's 1-3 foot height.
Great Stonecrop is much larger and more robust than its close relative Orpine, with bigger leaves and flower clusters.
